newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Holocaust plaintiff to confront Allianz.
newsitem.headline: Holocaust plaintiff to confront Allianz.

text.p: A Holocaust survivor who is part of a mass U.S. legal action against European insurers said she would take her claims to the Munich headquarters of Germany's Allianz AG on Monday.

Margret Zentner, 75, and her New York lawyer Edward Fagan on Sunday said they would present documents challenging Allianz's claims that Zentner was compensated in the 1950s by Germany as a person whose life insurance policies were stolen by the Nazis.
Zentner, whose German Jewish family in Frankfurt perished in the Holocaust, is claiming an unknown amount for an insurance policy taken out as a savings plan for her by her parents.
After a tussle with German authorities, Zenter and Fagan were given files on her case on Friday from the German Restitution Office, which keeps records on German compensation to Holocaust victims.
"Allianz will not be pleased at what is in that file. We will announce that tomorrow morning in Munich," Fagan told a news conference in Zurich where he and Zentner stopped on the way to Germany.

Fagan, who heads two class action suits in New York against European insurers and against Swiss banks over Holocaust assets, declined to be more specific about the file before the Monday news conference at the office of Munich lawyer Michael Witti.
After the news conference, Zentner said she planned to go to the Munich corporate headquarters of Allianz on Monday and seek a personal response.
"I certainly want to speak to the people from Allianz and see what they have to say," said Zentner, who emigrated to the U.S. after World War Two and now lives in Queens, New York.
Allianz is one of 16 insurers in Germany, Austria, Italy, Switzerland and France named in a complaint filed in Manhattan federal court in March by Holocaust victims and their families.
The suit claims the insurers cheated Nazi victims of billions of dollars of policies that were confiscated by the Nazis and then improperly transferred, liquidated or cashed in.
Allianz, while insisting that the bulk of claims against it have already been settled, has pledged to honour all reasonable outstanding claims.
The company is running a 24-hour hotline which descendents of victims of Nazi persecution can use to register their claims against the company.
Zenter said she had first written to Allianz in 1948 demanding her policy, which was supposed to be paid out when she turned 21 or married.
"The excuse they gave her was that they had paid it out to the (Nazi) SS and weren't paying out twice," Fagan said.
Nazi Germany required insurers to hand over Jewish life insurance policies under the racist laws that culminated in the mass murder of six million European Jews.
Fagan said Allianz later claimed that Zentner was paid under a German government program launched in the late 1950s to compensate victims of the Nazis for stolen insurance policies.
"They (Allianz) told me that, but I never received any," Zentner told reporters.
